May I make a remark on a question raised by the hon. member for North Cape Breton, that is, the supply of potatoes. He read a telegram from somebody in Quebec complaining of the shortage and asking what could be done to get potatoes, as they could not get them from New Brunswick. I told my hon. friend that I would secure any further information. We have dispatched .a large number of telegrams all over the country to the officials to try to obtain further information on that question. I have been informed by the Department of Agriculture in Nova Scotia that while there is no available surplus of potatoes there are probably enough for seed and for domestic use in that province. As to Saskatchewan, I have had a telegram from the Minister of Agriculture, in which he says:-
We have ascertained potato supply approximately adequate. We know of a few carloads for sale, and no acute shortage.
I have a telegram also from the Minister of Agriculture for Quebec only this morning, because Quebec was supposed to be suffering from a shortage:
I have not any precise information as to the exact quantity of potatoes in Quebec at present. Certain districts have slight surpluses, placing them in position to supply other districts where there is a shortage. But the quantity available to-day is very small. We have received several applications since a few days.
I have a telegram from Alberta which is not at all clear. Alberta reported a surplus in March of 800,000 bushels. The telegram I got was so vague that it did not make the matter clear, and I telegraphed again for further information.
The other western provinces, Manitoba and British Columbia, I have not heard from; I imagine that they have not more than enough for their requirements. The

only provinces, therefore, which are left, apart from Ontario, which is short, are New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. I am informed by telegram from official and unofficial sources that in New Brunswick there are probably now available for seed outside the province somewhere about 50,000 to 70,000 bushels, and that in Prince Edward Island probably 100,000 bushels will be available for the outside market, that is the rest of Canada. I have passed that information on to the ministers of Quebec and particularly to Ontario, where, of course, they are more or less in need.
It was stated the other day that we ought to take somewhat fuller steps, and I pointed out at that time that we considered the provincial machinery was so much more effective than ours in keeping them in close touch with the farmers through their district representatives, etc., that they would probably be able to deal with the potato question more effectively than we could, because it is entirely different from grain, which we can deal with through the officers of the Seed Branch. As a matter of fact, the Deputy Minister of Agriculture for Ontario was here early in March and informed us that he was taking steps, and I understand that recently they have been bringing in potatoes and doing what they can to relieve the districts which are short. It was stated in the paper the other day that Dr. Creelman, who has lately been appointed Commissioner of Agriculture, had said that I was trying to shift the responsibility from my shoulders. I very much question whether Dr. Creelman ever made such a remark. Indeed I understand that at about the time he was appointed he stated through the press some of the plans he had in contemplation in respect to these questions.
May I also say one word on a different phase of this subject, which the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Duncan Boss) intended to bring up in the House. My hon. friend spoke to me personally about the matter. A great many inquiries have been made as to whether the Government would do something in the way of guaranteeing the price of potatoes. Of course, this raises a very large question which could hardly be discussed at this time. The question of guaranteeing a minimum price is a very difficult one. England has guaranteed a minimum price of potatoes of about $30 a ton, or about 75 cents a bushel. England is threatened with an extraordinary shortage. She is a very heavy importing

country, whereas we are an exporting country of all agricultural products, including potatoes. In my province last year thousands of tons of potatoes sold at as low as $7 and $8 a ton, from 20 to 25 cents a bushel. If, therefore, under conditions of that kind the Government guaranteed a minimum price which would be regarded by some as fair, the Government might have to pay out on their guarantee from $10,000,000 to $20,000,000 on that one commodity. I think those who have looked into the matter agree that under conditions as they are now and promise to be, there is very little likelihood of the price of potatoes being such as not to afford ample remuneration to the farmer. With regard to the question as to whether we should fix a maximum price, I may say that I received to-day, from the same -district as that from which my hon. friend's telegram came, a long letter affirming that the Government should affix a price of, say, $1.50 a bushel, which the writer thinks would be a reasonable price. The House must know that the fixing of a maximum price on commodities is an extraordinarily complex thing. England has not attempted it on any large scale, though she may come to it. In Italy it has broken down; in Germany it has, to some extent, broken down. In the United States they are giving the matter the most profound consideration. Secretary Houston admitted only the other day that the fixing of maximum and minimum prices for foodstuffs would not be a wise measure except as a last resort. The question presents many difficulties; as the hon. member for Bed Deer has suggested, legislative action has often quite unexpected results, and fixing a maximum price might even tend to restrict production. After all, a high price is the very best spur to production, as it is also the very best spur to economy.
By your leave, Mr. Speaker, may I ask my hon. friend whether the Government sends the seed grain to the municipalities, or to the farmers direct?

First of all to the municipalities, and to the farmer direct as well. It is sent to the dealers and farmers as well as to the municipalities. In the east it is sent only in carload lots, because that is obviously the only possible way.
Is this done by the Government itself, or through the commission which was appointed?

Through the commission, acting under the direction of my department. Of course, we sell for cash. So satisfactory have been the transactions and so whole-hearted has been the co-operation of all the provinces and municipalities, that up to May 7, the Receiver General has received through our commission, by way of amounts paid in for the grain, no less a sum than $898,000.
I observe that my hon. friend has cited two or three Orders in Council which have not been brought down to the House. I think they should be brought down.
I had an idea that they had been brought down. If not, I shall be very glad indeed to lay them on the Table.

Has the hon. minister
any more grain available for seeding.
Oats and wheat are still available, though it would be rather late to get in wheat now from the West.

By your leave, Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out to the minister that some time ago he gave an interview in the course of which he said that there were in the country one or two million bushels of potatoes more than were required. He said this afternoon that there were not enough potatoes. Is that the case? In a farming community we are paying as high as $1 a pock for potatoes.

My hon. friend could not have been in the House the other day when I spoke about that. A considerable surplus was estimated early in March, but since that time a large amount of potatoes has gone out, attracted by the high price in the United States. The condition in the United States is exactly as it is here. Potatoes in the United States are worth $3 a bushel and even more; there is a big shortage. Because of the high freight charges from British Columbia to the East on such a heavy commodity as potatoes, naturally there would be a steady flow of that surplus from my province into the United States. I can not tell my hon. friend the exact amount that has gone out though the amount is large, or what the surplus is now, because I have not received definite word from Alberta, which is supposed to have a considerable surplus. Unquestionably the surplus of a million and a half bushels has been steadily melting away, and I question very much whether
there is now any or much of a surplus in the country. I think I have referred to the two provinces which have an available surplus.

My reason for making the inquiry is this: A great many potatoes were shipped to our section of the country from British Columbia and Alberta, but when the winter came on these shipments fell off, because the railway charge so much for a car for heating, and shipping becomes rather expensive. If there is still a surplus in British Columbia and Alberta, it would be a very good thing if the minister would let the country know about it. Potatoes are perishable, and any surplus might very well be shipped to the East.

I can only repeat what I have already said. We have given all the information that wp have received up to date. I wired to the Ministers of Agriculture for Ontario and Quebec this morning, informing them as to the conditions, and told them that as soon as I got fuller information from Alberta, it would be sent to them.
On the Orders of the Day:

I see my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence in his place, and I should like to call his attention to a matter as to which I made a private communication to him. I have bad a number of letters complaining of some apparent slackness in the way that the separation allowances arrive in the hands of the wives of men at the front. I understand that other members have had similar communications. In the 5 p.m. case of one correspondent a reply was made from the department that when a married man at the front is reported missing the pay is cut off for three months. That seemed to me to be a very peculiar thing to do, because no one would miss the man more than the wife he has left at home, and there would be no moment in her life when she would need the assigned pay more than in those three months. If it is in the slightest degree inconvenient to the hon. minister to reply now I am willing that he should postpone his answer. I am sure that a number of people in the country would be glad to know, in a short statement, the way separation allowance is granted, and to have the assurance that no distinction is made be-

tween one person and another in the carrying out of the regulations.

The administration of separation allowances and assigned pay is very intricate and difficult. It will interest all the members of the House and perhaps the public, if I make, with regard to the matter, a complete statement which will cover the whole situation as regards delays, alleged irregularities, and matters of a similar nature. The particular matter to which my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) has referred is that of a man who was reported missing and who had his pay cut off. No official notice would come that the man was missing until sometime after the event occurred, and just what action would be taken in this particular case. I cannot say. There are, in connection with the administration of separation allowance, almost - as many combinations as can be made out of the alphabet. Perhaps that is an exaggerated way of putting the case, but it will convey the idea that I have in mind. This is the statement to which I refer:
Separation Allowance and Assigned Pay.
There are now being issued monthly from Ottawa 150,000 cheques for assigned pay, and 90,000 for separation allowance, in all, 240,000 cheques each month. In the past, there has been some delay in getting the separation allowance cards and assigned pay rolls. It is estimated that this delay has occurred in 10 per cent of the cases, and varies from two to six months. If the pay officers were authorized to pay every one on their own application, there would undoubtedly be fewer complaints, but if this were done, a vast amount of public funds would be improperly paid out, as hundreds of claims are received every month, which, on examination and inquiry, are found to be invalid, or outside the regulations, consequently care has to be exercised when placing new names on the list.
Delay has resulted from many causes, viz.,
(a)	Inexperienced paymasters, particularly on
formation of battalion.
(b)	A sudden and large increase in the volume
of business.
(c)	Inexperienced clerical staff.
(d)	Difficulty in getting accurate and quick
information from overseas.
(e)	Soldiers neglecting to fill up separation
allowance cards or to make assignments of pay,-.in a great many cases for personal reasons.
(f)	Battalions suddenly ordered to proceed
overseas, and embarking without leaving assigned pay rolls, or any information respecting them. This has happened in a great many cases.
(g)	Instructions from overseas to stop payment ; usually no reason being given.
(h)	Change of address. Thousands of such
notices are received every month, and some women change their abode every few weeks, and often without notifying the department.

(i)	Incomplete information on the assigned - pay rolls or separation allowance card, necessitating correspondence often with the authorities overseas, if the battalion has left Canada.
Many regimental paymasters failed to do their duty in not ascertaining from the men themselves, by personal interview, whether they had dependents or not. They left it to the men themselves to make application for separation allowance, and to assign a portion of their pay. The result was that quite a percentage of the men in these units, either through ignorance or carelessness, did not make any application. The wife or the mother in the meantime was expecting her allowance, and perhaps some months afterwards would write complaining about it. It would then devolve upon the pay branch at Ottawa to make inquiries, which always takes time, and hence delay.
There has undoubtedly been delay occasionally in the pay branch at Ottawa, owing to inexperience or carelessness of clerks in the pay offices. There has been a great deal of difficulty in getting a competent staff, and often during the past eighteen months, a half a dozen of the best trained would leave at once to join an overseas unit. Many left also to take up permanent positions elsewhere, or because they were offered higher salaries, consequently there was always a very large percentage of absolutely inexperienced clerks. As a rule, however, the clerks have worked long hours and very diligently, and a very small percentage of the delays can be traced to them.
In considering this matter regard should be had to the great distance the force overseas is from Ottawa and as already stated the difficulty in getting necessary information quickly when the soldier concerned is in France or England. Moreover, a great many complaints are received as a result of stopping assigned pay. The instructions to stop payments are received from the overseas authorities, and such cases are very numerous. We have to comply with these instructions, as the soldier's pay account is kept in London, and all assigned pay issued here is charged against him there.
Another grievance is that when a soldier is promoted, action is not taken here at once to increase the separation allowance. The reason for delay is that it takes a long time to get this information from overseas; in fact it is usually necessary to write for it. The soldier, of course, informs his wife or mother immediately he is promoted, which, as a rule, occurs in the field, but the officer dealing with the promotion does not take action so quickly, and when he does, advises London office, which in turn should advise this office.
As an instance of delay, the very last application for separation allowance and assigned pay may be given. This particular case was presented through Mr. F. L. Schaffner, M.P. The facts are as follows: It is the case of the mother of Private P. B. Smillie, whose father died after his enlistment, and consequently the mother claimed separation allowance from that date, on the ground that her son was her sole support. The first letter received from her was in December last in which she stated that her son had enlisted in the 46th Battalion. The records of the 46th Battalion were fully gone over, and no trace of Private Smillie could be found thereon, and his mother was so informed. In her reply dated 19th January, she did not state which battalion he was in, but in a sub-

sequent letter received from her on the 21st January last, she stated he was in the 65th Battalion, not the 46th, as first stated. The nominal rolls of the 65th Battalion were examined, but there was no assignment shown thereon, and Mrs. Smillie was duly advised of this on the 1st of February. At the same time, the chief paymaster, London, England, was written asking if he would communicate with Private Smillie with a view of having him make such an assignment. On the 16th February last, a card for separation allowance from the chief paymaster, London, was received, and this card was forwarded to Reverend J. Hunter, Belmont, Manitoba, asking him to certify on the card that the soldier was the sole support of his widowed mother. On the 27th of March, authority was received from the chief paymaster to open an account for assigned1 pay at the rate of $15 per month from the 1st of February, 1917, and a cheque for February and March was forwarded by registered mail on the same day to Mrs. Smillie. Early in April last, the necessary certificate for separation allowance was received from the Reverend J. Hunter, Belmont, Manitoba, and separation allowance was granted from the 1st of April, 1917, and a cheque forwarded to Mrs. Smillie. On the 13th of April, Mrs. Smillie was advised that the matter was being considered as to whether separation allowance should be made retroactive. This is in accordance with the usual practice of the department.
Private Smillie evidently did not make any assignment until he proceeded overseas, and it was only after the chief paymaster, London, took up the question with him that he did make an assignment. This made it effective from the 1st of February, and not from a date prior to this, as claimed by his mother, Mrs. Smillie, moreover, in her communications to the department did not give her son's regimental number and corps, which, of course, necessitated a great deal of research, as without this information it is necessary to go through a great many thousands of files-there being some 300,000 of these in the registry. In her last letter, Mrs. Smillie makes the accusation that the delay in her case was undoubtedly due to their being a great number of "snobs" in the department, who were inattentive to their duties, whereas, the fault undoubtedly was due to her son not making any effort to obtain her separation allowance and assigning her half of his Pay, until the matter was taken up with him personally by the chief paymaster, overseas. It will thus be seen that the department took a great deal of trouble in order to get the matter adjusted. This case is cited as a very fair sample of the difficulties which the department are up against in dealing with these cases.
I have in my hand a pamphlet containing four army orders of the British army for April, and the British authorities are having in respect of this matter exactly the same difficulties that we are having here, but their difficulties are less complicated as the British authorities are, so to speak, on the scene, having large numbers of soldiers in England and being near France, whereas we are far away. Nearly two pages of this pamphlet are devoted to explanations of difficulties in the way of administering separation allowance, and in some
respects the difficulties are identical with those which I have just cited. We are all in the department very glad to answer any inquiries, but sometimes, before we can give a definite answer, we have to cable to Great Britain. The paymaster of a battalion may be a man inexperienced in keeping accounts; in fact, sometimes officers from the headquarters staff here follow battalions to Halifax to try to get their accounts straightened out and their separation allowance and assigned pay cards so arranged that the soldiers' relatives will get their money at the proper time. Sometimes we have to send officers over to England on the ships in order to get the accounts of some battalions straightened out, these officers returning to Canada on the .arrival of the vessels in England. The 'soldiers arrive in England, then they change their abode in England; they go to the front and their address is changed again. If they are unfortunate enough to be wounded, they are taken from one base hospital to another, then from France to England and from England back to Canada. Their wives and relatives here also change their addresses frequently. Delays are also occasioned by mistakes made by inexperienced clerks. We have in the department many invalided men who have devoted their energies to straightening out thei separation allowance branch and other branches of the department. In that Rranoh at Ottawa there are about 600 clerks employed, and one or two of the heads of that particular branch have already 'broken down through ill-health caused by over-work. - On the whole, however, I can assure my hon. friend from Red Deer that every effort is being made to improve the work of that (branch.

subtopic: AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS FROM THE UNITED STATES.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

subtopic: AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS FROM THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to call the attention of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Roche) to this telegraphic despatch that has appeared in some of the newspapers published in Prince Edward Island:
Chicago, April 26.-Five hundred students of the Agricultural College of the University of Illinois left here last night for Saskatchewan to help produce the war-winning wheat crop. The Dominion Government has guaranteed minimum wages of $50 a month and board, part of railroad fare, and 160 acres to all who serve six months in the fields.
I wish to ask tho miniater if the statements in this despatch aio correct or partly

correct. Perhaps he could tell me how many persons have been brought into western Canada from the United States for the purpose here mentioned, what privileges were extended to them, and whether similar privileges will be extended to persons who wish to go to the West from say the province of Prince Edward Island.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. J. ROCHE (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS FROM THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Some of the statements contained in the despatch are partly correct. There has, of course, been a very great shortage of agricultural labour in the western provinces, and the National Service Commission in conjunction with the Immigration Branch of the ^minion Government have taken the matter up with the governments of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta with a view to getting agricultural labourers from the United States. Our information was that there was a scarcity of labourers in other provinces of the Dominion, and we therefore could not look to the eastern provinces to supply labourers for the West, so an arrangement was made between the provincial governments and the Immigration Branch by which agricultural labourers coming from the United States could receive tickets at three points at the rate of one cent a mile. The three points were Duluth, St. Paul, and Spoibane, and the balance of the fare was to be borne equally by the government of the province to which the labourer went, and the Dominion -Government. The statement as to the granting of 160 acres is, of course, not correct. Any person has the privilege of taking up a homestead of 160 acres, and any person who does so this year will be allowed to- count the time which he spends with a farmer as an agricultural labourer, as residence on his own homestead; that is the extent of the privilege with regard to homesteads. The despatch is wrong in saying that there were 500 students, as my information is that on the 2nd of May there were only 196 or 197 students. I do not think it would be wise to extend the same privileges to farm labourers in our provinces, as our information is that nearly all the provinces are short of labour themselves. Of course, farm labourers from Prince Edward Island, or any other province, would he allowed to count the time they spent with a farmer, just as would these labourers from the United States, but they would not be granted the same privilege -as regards railway fare, because the railways in Canada would not make such an arrangement.

subtopic: AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS FROM THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: The telegram said that the Government was guaranteeing a minimum wage of $50 a month and hoard.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS FROM THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I omitted to say that the Dominion Government has not guaranteed any wage at all. The extra agents who have been sent to the United States by the Dominion -and Provincial Governments, six of them from Manitoba,'ten from Saskatchewan, six from Alberta, and a like number from the Dominion Government, would no doubt try to induce agricultural labourers to come here by telling them that the prevailing rate of wages was from $40 to $55 a month, but there was no guarantee at all.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext: With your permission, Mr. Speaker-, I will now resume my remarks on the Budget, which were interrupted by the adjournment of the debate last Friday. I am confronted now by somewhat different circumstances, for, instead of the Minister of Finance leading the House, we have now the Acting Premier himself, just returned from the Capitol of the United States, where it has been his lot to take counsel with the representatives of the three great democracies of the world. I am sure that the name and fame of Canada have not suffered through their representative the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce. I am sure he has been able to meet with the dignity becoming a representative of Canada, those great statesmen and orators of our Allies, and I fear that in coming back to this House his first task of listening to me will fall very heavily upon him.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext: I will suffer that willingly.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext:
I can not promise him that brevity which characterized the speech of the Minister of Finance in presenting the Budget. I have not that command of facts and figures that I can say much in few words. Moreover, I intend to deal with many subjects which are not in the Budget, but which, in my judgment, should have been. Although the right hon. gentleman who is leading the House is very properly giving his attention to international duties there are also duties for him in Canada,

for we are not supposed to neglect our duties at home while we are fighting for the Empire.
The Minister of Finance endeavoured to show the great prosperity of Canada by export and import figures. He showed that for the year ending March 31, 1917, our exports and imports aggregated $2,043,000,000, and the amount of revenue for the last four years was also given. The revenue for the year ending March 31, 1917, amounted to $232,000,000, of which $134,000,000 was derived from customs, $34,000,000 from excise, and $12,500,000 from the business profits war tax, which latter figure the Finance Minister hoped would amount at the end of the accounting period to $15,000,000. Out of this revenue the Minister of Finance has paid off the ordinary and capital expenditure of the past year, and has been able to apply $60,000,000 to the payment of our war expenditure, or about 10 per cent of the war expenditure so far. Before the outbreak of the war, our National Debt according to the Minister of Finance amounted to $336,000,000. It now amounts to $900,000,000, and before the end of the fiscal year the Finance Minister thinks it will likely reach $1,200,000,000. The minister tells us that the most striking aspect of our affairs is the increase in our international trade. And he gives the total of that trade for the year ended March 31 last as $2,043,000,000. He did not give a statement of the imports and exports, saying that he would prefer to give these figures in committee. But the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) tells us that in 1916 we sold to the outside world goods to the value of $1,178,000,000, and bought from the outside world $864,500,000 worth, an excess of exports over imports of $314,000,000. He informed us also that our exports of munitions might be estimated at $300,000,000, and said that, even deducting that amount, our exports would amount' to $878,000,000. But we must allow also for the greatly increased prices since the war, if we are to estimate fairly the increase in the quantity of goods exported. We find that our exports of bread-stuffs to Great Britain for 1916 were valued at $198,281,735, while those of 1915 were valued at $113,140,435, an increase for 1916 of $81,141,300. But the quantity of grain exported in 1916 was not much greater than that of the year before. This shows that the value of such exports was inflated by the increased prices. If the prices of the days before the war still prevailed, the value of our exports would be represented
by very much smaller figures than is the ease to-day. The Minister of Finance regarded our great foreign trade as a sign of prosperity in the country. During the recess of the House many members on the Conservative side, addressing meetings in their several constituencies, have cited these figures as evidence that the country is now enjoying greater prosperity than ever before. I have no doubt that they have placed these figures and this conclusion before their electors in all sincerity. But when we consider the cause of our present prosperity, 1 claim that it is not >a prosperity to gladden the heart of the true Christian, while it must sadden the mind of the economic thinker to contemplate the transition period which our country must face when the bugles sound for peace and we must seek a permanent basis for our manufactures and commerce. All winter in my own town I have observed the movement of the munitions trains on the railway toward our winter ports of St.- John and Halifax. I could not but realize that for every one of these trains that was moving over our lines the Huns were moving ten trains carrying weapons of destruction against the sons of Canada and against all the soldiers of the Allies. And I said to my neighbours:	These cars are
not the signs of progress, prosperity and happiness, but of universal grief and mourning. 'So we (must not depend upon the figures of our present exports of the weapons of destruction and the materials to make and load those weapons as assuring our prosperity, we must look to the future and not merely to present conditions which we know to be but temporary. As true Canadians we are willing to pay the debt which (is now accumulating because of this war. We face our responsibilities with courage, still ready to carry our sacrifices to the limit of 'which we have so pften spoken, " our last man and our last dollar," in order to insure victory for the Allies. When peace comes, we shall be ready, I hope, to do what the French people did in 1871 when they paid the immense indemnity which had been demanded of them, paid it in full and far in advance of the time allowed, in .order that they might be under tribute to their enemy for as short a time as possible. Even though our public debt should amount to nine or ten billions, we will remain Canadians and animated with the same principle of justice and Christianity for which we have battled in this war. For this is a fight for out liberties, it is a

fight R>r the principle of Christianity. And when the war has ended shall we leave the debt to be met by future generations? I believe that we should do everything in our power to meet, while we are living, as large a part as possible of the debt incurred in this war. To my mind, the additional war tax which the Minister of Finance has imposed should have been imposed last year, or two years ago, as was proposed by hon. members on this slide of the House. In order that I may follow more intelligently the remarks of the Minister of Finance, let me read this resolution:
Resolved, That it is expedient to amend the Business Profits War Tax Act, 1916, by providing :-
1.	That in any business taxable under the Act where the annual profits exceed fifteen per centum per annum the tax shall be increased to fifty per centum with respect to all profits in excess of the said fifteen per centum
_but not exceeding twenty per centum per annum, and where the profits exceed twenty per centum per annum the tax shall be increased to seventy-five per centum with respect to all profits in excess of the said twenty per centum, and such increases in the tax shall be levied against and paid by the person owning such business for each and every accounting period ending after the thirty-first day of December, one thousand nine hundred and sixteen;
2.	That for the purposes of the said Act, the actual unimpaired reserve, rest or accumulated profits held at the commencement of an accounting period by an incorporated company shall be included as part of its capital as long as it is held and used by the company as capital;
That any enactment founded on this resolution shall be deemed to have come into force on and from the eighteenth day of May, one thousand nine hundred and sixteen.
What I regret most is that it has not been made to date from May, 1915, instead of May, 1916. It was then that the largest profits were made by those making munitions. We all remember that after the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte), in his speech in this House, made the accusation that excessive profits were being made by some contractors and Government agents, many of these profits were curtailed. If for nothing.else, the hon. member for Richmond deserves the gratitude of the people of Canada in calling attention to these excessive profits. But this resolution, after all, allows the big corporations from 15 to 20 per cent on theiir paid up capital before they are touched by the Government taxation. In these strenuous times, and in the presence of this horrible war, the Minister of Finance should have grasped for the country the whole of the remaining percentage above that profit. Perhaps, as in the case of the war profits tax at the beginning, the imposition will fall most

heavily on the companies that have been operating with a small capitalization, and which therefore show larger profits. The large interests that have operated from the first and made large profits have generally issued sufficient stock in a'll denominations to increase their outstanding capital to such an extent that they seldom show a profit of 15 per cent, and, therefore, they will not be affected by this new proposition.
We have had suggested-and I have myself suggested-to the Minister of Finance that he should introduce an income tax in this country. The answer is that the revenue derived from an income tax would not amount to more than the expense of collecting it. That might depend on the basis that you adopt for the adjustment of that income tax. Meanwhile, I may say that I believe there are many people, and many classes of people, who should pay an income tax, and that such a tax would give to the country a revenue which would be available for the elimination of the war debt. The railway corporations would not be affected in their corporate capacity, I know, because there is no profit for them in the operation of their railways under war conditions, but our railway magnates have large incomes from other sources, which would be taxable and which would give a good return to the country. The property owners in the cities, as well as in country districts, who are in comfortable circumstances, might also pay an income tax. Some say that the farmer is the one man who will not stand such taxation. The farmer is just as devoted and as patriotic as any one of us in this country. Give the farmer the markets of the world, give -him what he needs for the operation of his great industry at the lowest possible cost and when he has reached the stage of comfort in his circumstances he will pay his income tax as well as his neighbour. Who has been more patriotic during the last three years than the farmer? Who has been of more service in carrying on the war, who has given more to the cause of civilization, than the farmers of Canada? Fifty or seventy-five per cent of the soldiers at the front have gone from the farms which, perhaps, to-day, are suffering from the want of then-labour.
I claim that taxation is more advantageous than loans because it eliminates interest on the amount you raise. If you raise by loan $10,000,000 to pay one item of expenditure during twenty years, at the end of twenty years you have paid $15,000,-

000 to clear off that expenditure. If you pay it by taxation, you take $10,000,000 from the people, the whole amount is paid and their ability to pay further is reserved for further needs of the country. I believe that is .a sound principle which could be applied with advantage to this country. If I buy a property for $5,000 or $10,000 and I have not the money to pay for it, I have to pay interest for ten years and at the end of that ten years I have paid out almost as much as the original debt. That same principle could be applied to all our expenditures and if it were you would avoid interest charges which equal sometimes the revenue the country collects. But, we have not been able yet to get from the Minister of Finance an answer with regard to this matter. May I be permitted to give an. example from the United States now that our hon. friends the Minister of Finance and the Solicitor General who, I do not see in their seats, are willing to truck and trade with the Yankees, inspired, perhaps, by different motives. The Solicitor General may be prompted by his humane feelings for the farmers of the West whom he will assure of his hearty sympathy when next he returns to the western provinces and the Minister of Finance by a consideration of war conditions. There is no doubt that the Minister of Finance and his friends, the manufacturers of Ontario, may be comforted by the hopes of the future, hopes upon which some light has been thrown by the hon. member for Chateauguay (Mr. Morris). However, now that we are permitted to look in that direction, may I be allowed to give these hon. gentlemen and this House a few facts with regard to the new income tax under consideration in the Congress of the United States and which is to be put into operation as soon as it becomes law. It is a bill for the further taxation of the incomes of individuals, corporations, joint stock companies, insurance companies and other possible incomes. They are taxing incomes as low as $2,000 in the United States. In Canada there axe a great many incomes of $1,000 which might be taxed. When a single man with no family to look after and no other responsibility but his own living, receives $1,000 under such conditions as prevail to-day, he will be proud, if he is a Canadian at all, to contribute out of his income a few dollars every year. If such a policy were adopted, the very minimum tax that you might place upon such incomes would represent a large amount of revenue every year. In the United States
it is a graduated tax upon all incomes, for instance, there is a tax of one per centum per annum on the amount by which the total net income is $5,000 or over and within $7,500, and of two per centum if the income exceeds $7,500 and over and so on up to $10,000. If a citizen has an income of $100,OOOhewill pay an income tax of $10,000.
A man having an income of $1,000,000 a year is taxed to the extent of $300,000. On an income of $500,000 a tax of $100,000 is paid into the treasury. This income tax, it is estimated, will provide for the United States Government $250,000,000 this year. You will see by the graduation of this income tax that every class will be called upon to pay according to its means. You will see that the United States have put a large income tax on millionaires. I might be told that millionaires in Canada are but few. I believe that they were not so few after all before the war. We had a good number, and I believe that since the war has commenced we have many more millionaires than before. It is only since the war that Canadian millionaires have beer; able to hand over hundreds of thousand* of dollars to young lady stenographers for past services, and I believe that it was not only in one case that this was done, that it will be found that many others acquired equal wealth as suddenly. Therefore both the old millionaires and the new millionaires, the new especially, should be taxed heavily under the conditions in which we are living, and I believe that if the Minister of Finance will look into the millionaires and dorei-millionair-es he will find enough of them in Canada to products millions of dollars of income tax. Britain is largely paying its war expenditure- by taxation. Germany is meeting it by loans, because Germany can not impose any more taxation. She had imposed so much taxation in preparation for war during forty years that her people were near rebellion, and when she.could impose no more taxation she declared war, the war which we are fighting to-day.
We have heard a good deal of discussion during the debate as to the relative merits of protection and free trade, or protection and tariff for revenue. It has always been a sad moment for me in this House when, on different occasions, I have heard members on the other side of the House, in order to propound the doctrine of protection, give us, for example, the great achievements of Germany under her system of ex-

treme protection in every possible direction. Last year the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) strongly advocated the imitation by Canada of German diplomacy in this respect, pointing to the wealth which the people of Germany had been able to amass through the facilities afforded to them for taking advantage of the opportunities for trade throughout the world. Lately the Solicitor General called the attention of Parliament and of the country to the great achievement of the German nation under her high tariff. Notwithstanding such pronouncements from the lips of those learned men opposite, I yet cling rather to the policy of Great Britain, which, during those same forty years, has built up a commercial and industrial activity which has enabled her, during the war, to save civilization. There is no doubt that in the first months of the war, civilization was saved by the superior tactics at the battle of the Miame by tlhe great man whom we honour to-day on this side of the Atlantic, General Joffre; but we can still claim that since that day the free trade policy of Great Britain has enabled her to save the situation for the last two years owing to her ability to finance not only herself but also France and all her Allies. To-day, with her navy, she is still saving the situation, while Germany is crippled, unable to move, and keeps up the hope of her people only iby the deceptive promise of the submarines, which we are bound to overcome with the assistance of the great nation to the south of us.

On section 1-Act of incorporation, 1914, c. 130, amended:
What are the amendments?

The Bill asks that the
privilege of using all the badges and other special marks of the Boy Scouts Assoeia-

tion shall be given only to the Boy Scouts. It asks, in effect, that these badges and other distinctive marks shall be a trade mark of the Boy Scouts Association.

That is all.

Yes.

Bill No. 10, to incorporate The Grand Lodge of the Canadian Association of Stationary Engineers of the Dominion of Canada.-Mr. F'ripp-in Committee.
On section 1-Incorporation:
This Bill is being asked for by the stationary engineers of Canada, both steam and electric.
Is there mutual insurance?

No, nothing of that kind. They are not asking for any control of the education or training of engineers. They merely ask that the Grand Lodge of the Canadian Association of Stationary Engineers be incorporated in order that the stationary engineers may be joined together for purposes which will raise -the standard of the profession. Certain amendments have been made, most of them of a minor character.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-executive officers:
Mr. MoKENZIE:	Is this an incorporating Bill coming before Parliament for the first time?

Yes, this is the original
incorporation.
Mr. MoKENZIE:	In the province of
Nova Scotia, and, I assume, in each of the provinces, there is an Act dealing with stationary engines and stationary engineers. I think that there is in the province of Ontario an Act requiring stationary engineers to pass certain examinations, and so on. Would this Act in any way come in conflict with the provincial legislation?

This proposed legislation
gives to the Grand Lodge no power whatever to license engineers. The province of Ontario grants licenses to stationary engineers, but this Bill is prepared in such a way that it asks for no rights or privileges which will interfere with those held or conferred by the provinces.

Section agreed to.
On section 8-objects and purposes:

In this clause the words
"and electric" are inserted after the word "etearn" wherever it occurs. The clause as amended reads in part: "the efficient operation of steam and electric power plants," and "steam and electric users."

Section agreed to.
On section 10-general meetings:	'

There is a slight amendment to that clause. After the word "as" in the third line, the words "the executive officers of" have been inserted, -making the sentence read:
The first general meeting of the association shall be held during the year 1917 at such time and place and upon such notice as the executive officers of the association may decide.

If I were a stationary
engineer I would w'ant that provision to be more explicit as to the time of meeting. Under that clause the executive could call a meeting within twenty-four hours. Were representatives of the -stationary engineers who attended the meeting of the Private Bills Committee in agreement with that amendment?

Yes.
Mr. MoKENZIE:	Is there any provision
for the making of by-laws?
Yes.
Are they subject to the approval of the Governor in Council, or is there any safeguard of that kind?
No.

It seems to me that
notice of, say, eight days should be given before a general meeting is called.

This clause refers only to the first general meeting of the Association, which is to be called by the executive officers of the Association. The subsequent general meetings shall be held annually as the by-laws of the Association may provide.
That covers the point.

Section agreed to.
On section 12-by-laws:

This section is struck out entirely owing to the fact that section 7 covers the matter. The section has relation to the making of by-laws.
On section 14-real estate:

To this section an addition has been made of a clause which has been inserted for some years in Bills similar to this. This section has reference to the amount of real estate which the grand lodge may hold. There is added after the words :-
Not exceeding in the aggregate tt'.e value of one nun red thousand dollars.
These words:-
And may sell, mortgage, lease or dispose thereof, but so that the association shall apply all its profits, if any, or other income, in promoting its objects, and shall not at any time pay any dividend to its members ; hut the provisions of this section shall not prevent the remuneration of members of the board of directors or officers of the association for services rendered out of any surplus remaining after the ordinary expenses of the association have been met.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported.
Bill No. 38, respecting certain patents of George C. Breidert and Burton W. Mudge.- Mr. Rainville-in committee.
Who is the promoter of this Bill-Mr. Macdonell?

The Minister of Agriculture left a memorandum on his desk and requested me, if he were not in bis seat when this Bill came up, to read it. This appears to be one of those cases where the application, through inadvertence, had not been filed in time, and the committee, after consideration, thought that it might -go through. The memorandum is a long one, and I will not read it -all, but it-says in part:-
In view of the foregoing facts and section 8 of the Patent Act, the commissioner has no power to deal with the applications. The object of the Bill is simply to empower the commissioner to deal with the applications as though they had been filed within the prescribed time. The facts as set forth in the preamble having been established by solemn declaration, and the committee being satisfied that the failure to file the applications within the prescribed time was due to an oversight of the Auto Utilities Manufacturing Company, considered that the petitioners were entitled to the relief asked for

and reported the Bill.' During last session a similar Bill, viz.: that of Mr. James W. Owen, was passed.
The minister says that the Bill has been gone over by the Deputy Commissioner of Patents, [DOT]and that he is satisfied with it.
Are any other rights interfered with?
No.
What are the patents for?

The Bill says that the patents are for ventilators.
On section 1-power to issue patents:

A certain amendment to this section ought to be noted. The words after " on the " in the third last line of this section are all struck out, and the words " 9th day of June, 1933," inserted, so that the date when the patent shall expire is made definite instead of being left indefinite as the original wording of the section left it.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-certain rights saved:

There are certain amendments to this section. The dates in the Bill as drafted are not inserted. The section as amended reads:-
If any person has since the 9th day of June, 1914, and prior to the 13th day of January, 1917-
And so on. The words " or construction " are added after the word " manufacture " in the fifth line, so that it reads " manufacture or construction in Canada." After the word " manufacture " in the third last Mne the word " construct " is added, so that the clause reads:-
May continue to manufacture, construct, sell and use-
And so on.

When the House adjourned at six o'clock I was endeavouring to show the fallacy of the policy which Germany has pursued for the last forty or fifty years, and which has brought upon her the misfortunes from which she is now suffering. Germany's policy of extreme protection has been the ruin of her prosperity. Capital and labour have been diverted from their natural productive employments into unprofitable and unproductive lines. Protection, to my mind, spells selfishness, egotism and defiance. Selfishness, in that it wishes to get for itself every possible profit at the expense of every other country; defiance, because it lacks confidence to meet other nations in equal competition. Free trade in itself implies brotherhood among the nations. In times of peace when Napoleon Bonaparte, who was a great civic father as well as a great general, found time to conduct the trade affairs of his beloved France, he always tried to make reciprocal treaties with the other nations of the world, but although he required the goods of England as much as the goods of any other land, he always refused to make a treaty with England because he abhorred that country. Germany abhors every nation in the world that she is not able to shackle, and I would advise this House and the country not to seek inspiration from the policy of the German people. The great emperor Francis Joseph, who perhaps had a longer reign than any other sovereign, unfortunately allowed himself to be captivated by the alluring prospects held out to him by Bismarck in the early part of his reign. Bismarck held out a prospect of battle and conquest, and the first step was. to Prussianize the universities of Austria, to divert the aims of education from the noble traditions of Austria-Hungary and adopt the system of education which has brought about the present catastrophe. This is no educational system for us. We should give no consideration to it at all or to their political, financial or industrial activities. We know what effect their education has had in corrupting the sentiments of the people and diverting them from humanitarian ideals. The industries developed under that education have marked their products " made in Germany." But though there was a. great increase in industrial production there was no increase in Christian education. And consider some of the things that have been "made in Germany." Poison gas to be projected across their
trenches to our lines where our soldiers fell by the thousand in agony; shells made to sink unwarned our hospital ships, with nurses and wounded, Germans among them; guns made to murder Edith Cavell because of her humanitarian activities-all these have been " made in Germany." Surely no lover of humanity, no Christian to-day who looks at the aims of . education in Germany will hold up that country as an example to the world' in -any respect whatever.
I wish to refer to another remark of the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) whom I am pleased to see now in his place. It may be considered that I am not in my place in coming into conflict with the hon. gentleman. He knows the high opinion I entertain of his ability. That ability is now universally recognized, but I am proud to say that I have appreciated from the day when he came into this House. I cannot close my eyes to the fact that, as it seems to me, sometimes his skill and subtlety in debate have been used in directions the contemplation of which in the future will not always bring him pleasure. Upon him has been placed the task of pulling the Government out of difficulties into which, from time to time, they have fallen. While recognizing his great talents, I cannot agree with his views on many questions, but especially upon questions, of the tariff. In the utterances to which I have referred he speaks of the increased duties made about a year ago, in Great Britain, on tea, coffee and chocolate, on clocks and watches, and on automobiles. As to the duties on tea, coffee, and chocolate, the object has been only increase of revenue, and not protection. When a tariff is imposed upon articles, whether necessaries or luxuries, the importation of which does not mean competition with home producers, the duties that are paid by the people go direct into the public treasury, while duties that are imposed for protective purposes go largely into the coffers of manufacturers. It is true also that duties were imposed on clocks and watches. But this was with a view of introducing economy. As to the duty on automobiles, it was designed ter save shipping tonnage which even then was growing scarce, and which was needed for the transport of munitions and food. Another reason for this duty, as stated by Mr. Asquith, the former Prime Minister, was that the duty would discourage the buying of automobiles in many cases, which would

have the advantage not only of promoting economy but also of saving gasolene and oil needed for the operation of automobiles used for war purposes. The Solicitor General also mentioned the dye industry and said that it could never be revived for the British Empire except by means of high protective duties. The modern method of producing dyes was the invention of an Englishman. This inventor could not convince the British Government of that day of the benefits that would result from his invention. So he went to Germany, and the Germans bought his secret and kept it as a secret. That has been their method in everything-to maintain secrecy. Their widespread secret service, for instance, was never suspected until war broke out. It was by keeping their operations secret that Germany was able to command the markets of the world in the dye industry. This was one of the mistakes made by the British Government, and governments make mistakes just as individuals do. It is only twenty-five or thirty years ago that the Liberal Government of Ontario offered to the Government of Great Britain control of the nickel properties of this province. But this was in a time of peace, and, unfortunately, the advantages to result from such a measure were not realized by the British Government of that time, and consequently the offer was refused. That such things will happen all history attests. Napoleon Bonaparte was approached by Fulton, the American inventor of the steamboat. Fulton went to France and securing the support of some of Napoleon's generals tried to convince the great Corsican of the benefits to be gained by the use of his invention, pointing out that by the use of steam the would-be conqueror of England could send ships across the Channel in a few hours, regardless of the weather conditions. But Napoleon replied that he had fools enough in France without importing them from abroad. Fulton went to England and had his invention adopted in that country, leaving to Napoleon only the remorseful recollection of an opportunity lost. As to the dye industry, when the war is over the scientists of France and England will seek out new chemicals which will be as advantageous and as profitable to commerce generally as the old secret has been to Germany.

May I say to the Solicitor General that if every grievance in the different parts of the country is to be appeased in that way, he might have come down to New Brunswick and given us free potatoes also. The farmers of New Brunswick would have been better pleased to have received a little less for their potatoes and to pay less for the flour or the boots they have to buy. A farmer has to sell three or four barrels of potatoes in order to secure a barrel of flour, even today when he gets $3 or $4 for his potatoes. Then he has to sell two or three barrels of potatoes to get a pair of boots for himself, or his wife, or his son helping him on the farm. The Government, under the Underwood tariff, had power to place potatoes on the free list on the same conditions as wheat, and my hon. friend could just as well have included potatoes in the Order in Council. How could it interfere with the independence of Canada when Canada and another country

come together and say: We will give you this product provided you give us the other product. It was a quid pro quo in every sense of the word. In the Maritime Provinces the people interested in the lumber business and the fish business suffered intensely during the two or three years subsequent to 1911. This was the condition until a year or two ago, when the trade with Britain was revived by the necessities o'f war. The consumer who formerly had to pay 50 cents a barrel duty upon his flour, under the new arrangement get6 his flour free. Under the reciprocity pact the consumer would have got his meat, his potatoes and his vegetables free. It is .a matter of necessity that the consumer should get his food free, particularly during those seasons when we do not produce the necessary food supplies in our own country. The advantages of that
proposed arrangement have not been properly appreciated; only to-day are some of the people realizing what we have lost by not accepting it. The West has lost a large portion of its farming population. Immigrants who bad come from the United States went back to their native land in hundreds and thousands. A large immigration would have been coming into Canada every year since 1911 but for the rejection of the reciprocity proposal. Its rejection caused a depression among the farmers of the West and a decrease in production has been apparent ever since. Had the reciprocity proposal been in operation when war was declared, we would have had an additional 100,000 farmers in the West to produce wheat and grain and food of all kinds. Through the rejection of reciprocity, the farmers of the prairie West suffered a loss of $25,000,000 on their crop of 1911, owing to congestion of traffic and lack of transportation, their grain remaining out and depreciating in value. , In 1912 the Minister of Trade and Commerce himself had to make arrangements with the United States authorities for certain transportation facilities in order that he might allow the wheat of the West to reach the ports of the United States.
We are told that the reciprocity arrangement would have been an interference with the fiscal independence of Canada. I do not appreciate the force of that argument. The reciprocity agreement would have been adopted by the people of Canada but for the exploitation of prejudices in Ontario and Quebec, arguments having been advanced in these two provinces designed to influence the unguarded electors in each.
We are asking the Government, through the amendment of the member for Assini-boia, to give to the Order in Council granting free wheat to the farmers the effect of permanency. The farmer of the West always looks to the future. He is interested in the war as much as any one in the cities of Montreal ot Toronto, his heart is set upon winning the war as quickly as possible. He is getting the benefit of the American market and of the markets of the world for his wheat, but he does not know what is going to become of that Order in Council when the war is over. We are told that it has the same effect as an Act of Parliament, but the farmer of the West will never believe that the same degree of permanency is afforded by an Order in Council under the War Measures Act as is secured by an Act of Parliament, which



could only be abrogated by another Act of Parliament. If the war is over before the farmer of the West can reap his crop next fall, he will not know how he stands in the matter of a market for his wheat. He knows that if he has access to the markets of the world, he will be able to compete in them, hut if he has to depend upon the markets of Canada he will be poor in the midst of plenty. It is said that it is better for the farmers to have the benefit of good prices temporarily, but what about the future? If the farmer of the West is assured that he will have free access to the markets of the United States and of the world, he will know that at all seasons he will be able to enjoy the benefits of those markets, and can govern himself accordingly.

I wish to refer now to the shipping industry, in regard to which the people of Canada are to-day very much agitated. We have recently heard a great deal of the necessity of reviving the ship-building industry in Canada. I wish that industry had been revived six or seven years ago; I wish it had been revived when the people of Canada and this Parliament were unanimous as to the project of building a Canadian navy in Canadian ports by Canadian workmen for the protection of Canadian commerce. Some years ago we heard our friends on the other side arguing as eloquently as any hon. member on this side for the establishment of a Canadian navy. When my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce introduced his resolution in 1909, we all listened to him as he waxed eloquent over his subject, and as his speech progressed and he was demonstrating the feelings of Canadians, he carried me with him into lofty heights of patriotism. He spoke of the mineT carrying from the bowels of the earth, of the coal and the iron ore in the blast furnaces where Canadian engineers and Canadian workmen were transforming the iron ore

into steel for the construction of Canadian ships, and he demonstrated to this Parliament the advantage of our commerce travelling side by side with its protector- a Canadian navy-across the sea. During the last six years, however, and more particularly during the last three years, Canada has produced the commerce but Britain has produced the protector. That is the state of things owing to the change of mind on the part of my right hon.'friend and his supporters on the other side who refused to accept the Laurier Navy Bill, as it was called, and therefore refused to give Canada and the British Empire the advantage of those ten cruisers which were to be built. Although at that time they were looked upon as a tin pot navy, the experience derived during the war prove that they would have been the best possible gift to the British Empire and to the British navy. When war was declared, we would have had some of those cruisers ready to defend from German warships the Pacific coast, where the people took freight, removing their bonds and gold from the bank and hiding them in their cellars, and where the local Government rushed to buy two submarines in order to defend the coast. Had the Liberal policy been accepted by hon. gentlemen opposite, submarines would have been built in Canada by Canadians. It is with sorrow that I say that during these last three years of war the Government has taken no steps to remedy the position of Canada so far as shipbuilding is concerned, and that it has not up to this date made any effort to build a single warship for the assistance of Great Britain. We see Australia, who has a treaty with us whereby our cruisers were to assist theirs in defending our trade on the Pacific coast, doing her duty and carrying off the honours of the war, and at the same time, in the absence of our Canadian cruisers, having to call upon the cruisers of Japan to come to her rescue.
However, better late than never. Like many another step we have urged hon. gentlemen opposite to take, it has been taken at last, but very late in the day. At the very beginning of the war we suggested that the Government should take over the Transcontinental shops at Winnipeg, Quebec and Moncton for the manufacture of munitions of war at cost price, thus saving the British Government millions of dollars. But they refused to do it. The British Government sent out Lord Rhondda to investigate the shell business in Canada, and he
endeavoured to persuade the Canadian Government to nationalize these shops, but nothing came of it. The Minister of Railways and Canals at one time seemed to have been influenced by the suggestions of Lord Rhondda, but after consultation with his colleagues, I presume, he told Lord Rhondda that he had no data on which he could fix a price.
I believe the time has come when we should give more attention to the building of ships. It is true that by an agreement with the United States, who have now become our Allies, that country is to build ships for the protection of commerce and. to replace the tonnage sunk by the German submarines. The daily shipping losses are certainly large enough to attract the attention of this Government. I have always been in favour of shipbuilding in this country. I think that if from the beginning of the war the shipyards of Vancouver and Victoria and Halifax and St. John had resounded with the incessant reverberations of the smith's hammer, it would have had a most potent influence on recruiting. I would urge the Government to encourage the building not only of steel ships but of wooden ships. Wooden ships, of course, do not afford so much protection, but they will be of immense value to Canada after the war. When peace is restored other nations will be coming along to buy	our	steelships as fast as we	can	build
them, but the wooden ships will remain our own property to be used in our coastal and perhaps trans-Atlantic trade. I trust the Government will make every effort to satisfy the Canadian people that they are doing their utmost to win this war as speedily >as possible. Every Canadian today is determined to do his part, but if we .want to w.in the war we must not depend upon the patriotism of the people alone. Canadians command the admiration of the world to-day. In the first year of the war they enrolled in hundreds of thousands, just as fast as the militia authorities could accept them. Canadian women have also done splendidly, and have shown great patriotism. In this the third year of the war Canadian women from the Atlantic to the Pacific are making every possible sacrifice. After giving a son or husband to the cause they are working night .and day for the comfort of our soldiers, helping the Red Cross and Patriotic funds, watching and praying for victory and the return of loved

ones. Let me tell you, Sir, as a representative of the Maritime Provinces, that in this great harmonious concert of virtues the Evangeline of to-day in the Maritime Provinces has revealed herself a worthy sister in nobility, patriotism and devotion. Let us pray that that will continue.

I do not know where the idea originated, although the ex-Mmister of Militia attributes it to the Prime Minister himself, 'but I know the opinion has been expressed in the Conservative and independent press, that the man who was working in a munition factory or on a farm was doing his duty just as much as the soldier in the trenches. When I think of the 400,000 young men who have gone overseas, I am filled with admiration for the Canadian youth; they have done well, but I do not say that Canada has done enough. It makes me mad to see the number of young men going into our movie shows; hundreds of thousands are wasting their time in these places when they should be in the factories or at the front, and I think the Government should take some steps to empty these theatres of our young men, so that their brothers in the trenches could be relieved for a while.
I say that Canada has done well, but Canada must continue to do well until the end. As one who believes that Canada cannot do too much in this great cause, and who is willing to accept everyone who may have failed in his duty in days gone by, hut is willing to tender that duty to his country now, I feel it my painful duty to mention the Teport that appears in the daily papers to the effect that there was disturbance at a public meeting in Montreal addressed by Hon. Mr. Blondin, now

colonel of a French-Canadian battalion. With the many and varied elements in a great city like Montreal differences of sentiment and of opinion are not unlikely to be found. Yet I believe that the disturbance in the meeting to which I have referred was the work of a very small number of persons, as compared with the great audience that had assembled. I confess, however, that I fear the effects that the report of such disturbances will have upon the mind of the world at large and of Canada in particular. It will be said that the French-Canadians of Quebec have forgotten their duty. Speaking as a French-Canadian, I yield to no English-speaking person in my patriotism, and in my loyalty to British institutions. I realize that under Providence it is to these institutions and their successful working in Canada that the French Catholic subject owes the liberty of speech and of worship which he has enjoyed. It is to the effect of British liberty upon public sentiment that we owe the fact that the false doctrines of the French Revolution have not invaded our country. So, as I say, I fear that the reports of disturbance at the public meeting to which I have referred will be interpreted against my race. I am not here as a representative of Quebec, but I am of that province native born, and I am jealous of its reputation. As I have said, I am willing to accept the return of anyone who may have misinterpreted French-Canadian sentiment in the past and now has changed his opinion, but I cannot but feel that these disturbances at public meetings are the residue of the false doctrine propounded by certain hon. gentlemen on the other side of this House in 1910 and 1911, when they preached that Canada owed nothing to the Empire and should not participate in her wars, or give her assistance in time of danger. The effects of the sentiments then inculcated cannot at once disappear, but let us hope that these effects will not last much longer. I trust that this untoward incident will not be represented as indicating that French-Canadians do not share the loyalty of their fellow-citizens. I trust that when called upon they will do their duty by enlisting under the command of Colonel Blondin, or anyone else who is sent upon similar duties, and that the province of Quebec will no longer be afflicted with reports which convey so false an impression of the sentiments of the people of that province.

The hon. member for Gloucester invited comparison in regard to Canada's debt, revenue, expenditure, trade, etc., between the record made by the party which he supports when it was in power and that made by the party which is now holding the reins of Government. I wish to take up that challenge briefly and first let me refer to that which we have always had in Canada, namely, the national debt. The national debt of Canada was increased by the Liberals during the fifteen years that they were in power by $87,000,000. The national debt was' increased during the last three years that the Liberals were in power by $62,250,000. There is some little explanation for that if you look back and note events in Ontario. In 1905 the Liberal Government in Ontario went out and the Whitney Government came into power. You might wonder how that would affect the Federal situation. It was in this way that the grafters and hangers on who had loaded themselves on the Liberal party of Ontario for the last ten or fifteen years they were in power, finding themselves out of a job in the provincial arena, -proceeded to besiege the fortress in Ottawa, and the party in power, the Liberals, could not refuse them. The result was that, following the election of 1908, when the Liberal party, the Laurier Government were returned to power in this country, they

thought that they were invincible, and they became absolutely recklesss in their extravagance and expenditures. With the fiscal year ending 1909 this party, which had denounced the Tory Government for extravagance, added $46,000,000 to the public debt of Canada in one year. In the next fiscal year, ending March 31, 1910, they added $12,500,000 to the public debt, and in the next year, 1911, they added $3,750,000, or a total addition to the national debt of Canada in the last three years of Liberal rule of $62,250,000. Then Providence very kindly intervened to save this country from those who were despoiling it, and up to March 31, 1914, the Borden Government had not only met its obligations, paid its expenses as it went along, but had shouldered some $120,000,000 of obligations incurred by the Grits while they were in power, and had reduced the debt from $340,000,000, what it was when they assumed the reins of office, down to $336,000,000. That was before the war broke out. Then the war came on and we have this to say, and I challenge contradiction of the correctness of my statement, that from the time the Borden Government assumed the reins of office, so far as the national debt of Canada is concerned, it has decreased that national debt by several millions of dollars, and that to-day we on this side of the House are in a position to say that not one dollar of debt has been added to the national debt of Canada since this Government came into power except through the war. During the last fiscal year not only did the Government meet all its obligations, current and capital expenditures, and meet a large pension call upon its funds, hut it also paid the interest on the national debt, and do not forget that in paying interest on the national debt they were paying interest on some $87,000,000 added to that debt by
10 p.m. the Liberal party. In addition to paying all this during the last fiscal year, this Government paid some $60,000,000 on war account.

That was the amount of our aggregate trade for the last year the Liberal party was in power. The first year after the Conservatives came into power, that is the fiscal year ending March 31, 1912 the aggregate
trade of Canada had increased from $752,000,000 to $841,000,000. The next year, 1913, it had still further increased to $1,063,000,000. Figures furnished by the United States Department of Agriculture, which is now as interested in promoting food production in the United States as is our own government here in Canada, place the number of men removed from productive pursuits by the war at 56,000,000. The figures of the food grains of the world, I am informed, up to March 31 of this year, showed that they were 150,000,000 bushels short of the world's requirements up to the month of August. That is the situation that we are in and it does not seem at all remarkable that there should be such a marked increase in the price of grain.
With regard to the price of flour, if hon. gentlemen will take the statement made by the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll), if they will take the statement made by the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) and if they will look these statements over very carefully, or even casually for that matter, and compare the trices of wheat with the prices of flour at

If you assume that it takes five bushels of wheat to make a barrel of flour, the price of flour conforms very closely to the price of wheat. It is folly to talk of forcing the millers to sell flour at a certain price without touching the price of grain. In order to reduce the price of flour you have to go back to the man who raises the wheat and force him to sell his wheat at a certain price. There is not an hon. gentleman on the other side of the House who will dare get up and advocate any such thing and fix the price. These hon. gentlemen will travel all around the price, but yet they say that the Government should commandeer the wheat. They take mighty good care to steer clear of fixing the price. They axe playing a double game in this as they have played a double game all along and as they played it in 1911 when they told the consumers that if they got reciprocity they would get everything for nothing and the producers that if they got reciprocity they would get higher prices for everything they had to sell.
1 am in hearty accord with the statement made by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), and I think some other hon. gentlemen, with regard to the taxation of war profits. We are approaching the time, or we have come to the time, when wealth has got to contribute more largely than it has in the past towards the expenses of this country. I think that taxation of war profits is a step in that direction, and I hope that in the years to come those who have accumulated large quantities of wealth will by legislation be made to contribute more largely than they have in the past towards the running expenses of our country.
