I cannot admire a leader who pledged his word to conserve the public domain of this country and who allowed his party followers to rob and steal from the public domain grazing lands, timber limits, and so on. I cannot express any great admiration for a leader who said: No coercion, so far as Manitoba was concerned, and who fastened the shackles on Alberta and Saskatchewan. Nor do I approve the course of a leader who said "hands off" one province; and would take another province by the throat, as he gave evidences of doing last session.
I have no great admiration for a leader

who posed as a man desiring interprovincial amity and concord, and has encouraged his compatriots to the verge of revolution. Nor do I admire a leader who said that he would not seek to open the doors of office writh a bloody key, and has smiled approval on tactics which have encouraged the enemy, retarded enlistment, and were intended solely to serve party ends. That, I think, is a fair indictment of the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition.
A good deal has 'been said as to whether or not we should have an election; as to whether or not there should 'be an extension of the life of Parliament. Well, Sir, if there is to be no extension of Parliament, the reason for not granting an extension must be found in such events as have taken place since the last extension of Parliament was granted. The first persons we should consider in this matter are the soldiers. The British Columbia elections demonstrated the impossibility of asking the soldier to vote over in the trenches. It would be a disgrace to the Dominion of Canada if an election were held at a time when it would be impossible to poll the soldiers' vote, because if there is one person more than another who has the right to express an opinion at the next election, it is the man who has gone overseas and is to-day risking his life in this war. But to any one who follows the press, other reasons are obvious why it would be inadvisable to hold an election at the present time. Speaking from a party standpoint, I would certainly say, bring on your election. But there is something bigger than party. Perhaps hon. gentlemen have read in the papers about what took place in the city of Montreal the other night at a meeting which one of the members of this Government tried to address. Any person who brings an election on in Canada at	this
time is assuming a grave responsibility, for I firmly believe that the adoption of such a course would result in bitterness which would not die out during the lifetime of any man who sits within the four walls of this building. Let those who wish to assume that responsibility assume it. One cannot help being saddened, as the hon. member for Gloucester said this evening, by the spectacle presented in Montreal the other night. A minister of the Crown seeks to impress upon the audience the importance of their duty in regard to the war, and he is hooted and jeered at and howled down by young men in that audience who evidently do not wish to listen to any ap-
peals along the lines of recruiting or enlistment. The reason for this, Mr. Speaker, is clear. The man who is responsible for the condition of affairs that exists in the province of Quebec is the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition. Follow the right hon. gentleman's career back as far as you wish and you will find expression after expression, statement after statement, made use of in times past by the right hon. gentleman which had a tendency to weaken regard for British institutions in certain parts of Canada. The right hon. gentleman sowed the wind, and we are reaping the whirlwind. His teachings, more than any other cause, are responsible for conditions prevailing to-day in the province of Quebec -and sad conditions they are.
Almost fifty years have passed since Confederation. There were big men in those " days, though they had their differences, just as men have their differences to-day. I suppose there were some little men in those days also, but a sufficient number of men were big enough to lay aside political differences and political ambitions in order to effect a great purpose. There is a great purpose before the people of Canada tojday, which demands that public men should lay aside their differences and their aspirations, and that purpose is the winning of the war. If the men who figured in the public life of Canada in days gone by could come upon the scene to-day what would they say? They would be filled with pride to see Canada taking its place side by side with Britain and France in this great struggle for liberty. I venture to say that men of ' the stamp of Howe, Tupper -and Tilley would not approve the attitude of the Carvells and the Kytes. I venture to say that men of the stamp of Blake and Macdonald and Mackenzie would not endorse the attitude of men like the Turriffs. And, Mr. Speaker, men like Cartier would not endorse the attitude which the right hon. leader of the Opposition has taken since the war began. These men, I say, were big enough to bury their political differences and to lay aside their aspirations in order to effect a great purpose, the Confederation of the Canadian provinces. But to-day we have men who for party and partisan reasons are risking the future of the community by encouraging a condition which has brought a part of our population almost to the verge of revolution. This is not as it should be, and I greatly deplore it. It does not matter very much whether a Tory Government remains in power or whether a Tory Gov-

ernment gives place to a decent Liberal Government-and I am not going to say that you could not find, if you searched diligently throughout the country, enough decent Liberals to form a Government. But, Sir, what does matter is this: it is very material to the future of this Dominion that the next Government which holds the reins of office should be in sympathy with Britain and with the British Empire, and should not be composed of the antiBritish and the foreign element in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, (the
deputy speaker, Mr. Riainville, in the chair) I followed with close attention the address just made by the honourable member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) and it is my intention in due course to reply to what he said about me in his closing remarks.
The Opposition had some cause for surprise in this year's budget. The Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) gave us free wheat. My only regret is that he did not go the whole way. I welcome his repentance; it is something in the right direction. Last week the Minister of Finance stated that with wheat on the free list the western farmer might secure a higher price for his wheat and the consumer purchase it at a lower cost. My honourable friend from Frontenac does not seem to .share that opinion, as for me, I do think, with the Minister of Finance that free wheat will be a boon to the farmers.
My object is to discuss shortly the situation of the farmers in the East. If, on his return from Washington, the Minister of Finance announced that hay would be allowed into the United States free of duty, 1 should congratulate him in the name of the Eastern farmers. This year free hay would be of more consequence than free wheat, because wheat is selling very well while the .price of hay is very low, there being no market for it. The Department of Agriculture at the beginning of the war had bought large quantities of hay in Quebec, but this year very few orders were placed, so that with the British market closed, we have only the American buyer to look to. If the duty of $2 per ton were taken off, it would help that much the export of hay to the neighbouring states.
I am sorry that the Minster of Trade iand Commerce (Sir George Foster) is not in his seat at present, but I hope that some of his colleagues present will advise him to take steps to obtain free hay for Quebec and a good part of Ontario.
I am always taken aback when I hear reciprocity discussed in this House. It is true, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Finance admitted that free wheat would result in more money for the fanners. On the other hand, he was taking to task the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfred Laurier) because in 1911 the Liberals had a different policy for different localities, because, said he, you told the farmers that with reciprocity the produce of the farm would fetch a higher price and in the city constituencies the candidates told the electors that goods would fall in price. The conclusion is quite logical, both the city and the farm would be benefited. The Minister of Finance 'states that free wheat means money for the farmers; he must then admit that free hay would mean the same to the Eastern farmer. If now butter, cheese, vegetables, all the fruits that we do not grow in winter, eggs, etc., were on the free list, the people in the cities would be the gainers. Is it not true that right now and through the winter, Canada has imported from the United States fruits and vegetables in very large amounts and millions of boxes of eggs, on which we have to pay a duty of three cents per dozen. So with butter and cheese. If there were no duties on such products, some kind of competition would be introduced, not against the farmers, but against the speculators, against those who store up those goods to. raise prices. Consequently, reciprocity with the United States in the exchange of the fruits of the soil would be of equal benefit to the country and the towns.
To me the reply of the Minister of Finance to my hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) on this question of free wheat was no small cause of surprise. The hon. minister apparently has a deep regard for the farmer's interests; nothing better; but I think the Government might have found a different answer for my hon. friend from Richmond. According to the minister's own statement, the situation is without remedy; the Government is powerless. The responsibility, said he, rests with the Imperial Purchase Commission. I claim, Mr. Speaker, that the Government could secure what they want if they had at heart the people's interest. But it must be taken into account that the common people who are in greater need of bread than the well-to-do, are not always in touch with the Government. It is not from the people that the Government springs, but the real rulers are the big wigs, not only the ministers, but the magnates that, surround them. Gould not an in-



vestigation find out in a very few days the quantities of wheat piled up in elevators, how long they have been stored -and the prices at which it has been bought? Then, allowing for the cost of storage, the interest on the investment and a fair profit on the cost price, the Government would have been in a position to say: we commandeer so many bushels of wheat for the people of this country.
What difference does it make whether it is the Imperial Government, the speculators or the millers who corner the wheat? The Government's first care should be the interest of the people who appoint them and I submit that it is not fair to let the people of this country suffer for the sake of the Imperial Purchase Commission. If I am rightly informed, very few goods are shipped overseas, because we have no ships and there lie one hundred million bushels of wheat stored up or in the hands of the growers. Why not in that case take from those speculators twenty or twenty-five million bushels at a little over cost price and have it milled in order to distribute the flour among the people at a reasonable price? The thing is as simple as a, b, c. The matter, Mr. Speaker, is where it always is: the big fellows must not be interfered with. Here is an instance: during the month of December, 1915, the Government put an embargo on Canadian wheat, prohibiting its export to the United States. They had a right to do so and I raised no objection because the big speculators cannot corner hay as they do wheat. Hay is not listed on the Exchange, as it is too bulky and cannot be stored up like wheat, and it takes too long to make millions out of it.
On the 23rd of February, 1916, in the course of my remarks on the Budget, I warned the Government that they might be right in placing an embargo on hay provided they took over the supply of No. 1 hay from the farmers of the province of Quebec and elsewhere, otherwise the embargo was ill-advised. You know the facts, Mr. Speaker, and at the time you yourself inquired as to the quantity of hay purchasable. I told you then that there were 55,000 tons of hay ready for shipping in the Maritime Provinces and all the way to lake Superior, and the Government required 100,000 tons. I further stated that in my constituency and elsewhere there would be some hay left over from last year when the new crop was ready for the market. Have *'my calculations turned out true or wrong?

Many members could find out from their electors that my statement is correct. The embargo was maintained until June, 1916. The Government, apparently aware of their mistake, raised the embargo but for a few weeks only.
What was the effect of the embargo on the hay dealers? They lost large amounts; the time being limited, they exported too heavily to the United -States. Hay is not like ordinary merchandise; the farmers must empty their barns to make room for the new crop. So with the dealers; their sales and consignments to the United States were too heavy -and, as a result, they lost $50 to $75 on every carload. Many kept their hay, and it brings $10 a ton to-day. And all that time, Mr. Speaker, our Government was buying hay from the United States. They paid no heed to the suggestion I had made on the 23rd of February, 1916, but went to Ohio, Michigan and New-York -State for hay for which they paid $20 a ton, although it was nothing but culled hay, that would have fetched barely $12 in New York and Boston or, I dare say, on any other American market. Hay sells well in the United States provided it is of good quality. The hay dealers of Ohio an-d Michigan arranged to sell to Canadian dealers-who resold to the Government at a profit of $5 a ton. I state without hesitation that profits were made amounting from $100,000 to $125,000 to .the detriment of the Canadian farmer who was debarred by the embargo from shipping to the United States.
, Now, Mr. Speaker, all this talk by Government supporter-s, about the country's prosperity being greater than ever before comes to me as a surprise. Let us investigate the facts. For instance, the Minister of Finance heralded that $134,000,000 were collected in customs duties from the people of this country. Does that indicate that we have been buying more than before the war? I think not: an imported article valued at say $40 in pre-war days and paying 30 per cent duty brought into the treasury $12; that same article is now valued at $80, $00 or $100, so that the same duty of 30 per cent increases the revenue by $30 instead of $12 with the additional 7J per cent war tax; thus three times more duty is paid on the same article than was paid some years ago.
-Shall we quote the high price of living, which has doubled or trebled, as proof of the country's prosperity?
Again, the manufacture of steel for war munitions has greatly increased the total production, but that, I think, will end with

the war. As a farmer and a business man, I claim that in our estimate of the country's business, we should not take into account our output of shells and munitions and other things necessary for our soldiers, the cannon fodder, as they were labelled in 1910-1911. When the war is over, the Minister of Finance and the Government supporters will find it impossible to boast throughout the country about the country's prosperity. The people see through the misleading statements made by the Minister of Finance and spread broadcast about the country.
Now for my hon. friend from Frontenac (M. Edwards), who saw fit to compare the liberal Government in 1896 with the present regime. It was terrible to have such a man as the Right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) at the helm for fifteen long years, from 1896 to 1911. Let us see. What was the national debt at the advent of the Liberal party in 1896? The net debt amounted to $258,000,000 and on the 21st of August 1911, it had increased to $318,000,-OOP; in 1896 the gross indebtedness was $362,000,000 increasing to $474,000,000 on the 21st of October, 1911; so that during fifteen and one-half years of Liberal rule the net debt has increased by $60,000,000 and the gross indebtedness by $112,000,000. Will you call that extravagance? If so, it is far less than under the present Government, with a great deal more to show in development of the country. From 1878 to 1896, Canada remained at a standstill, while it made gigantic strides from 1896 to 1911, with no expenditure for military purposes. Hon. gentlemen opposite blame the war for their enormous Budget and claim all the credit for an increased revenue.
Suppose a farmer lives on his farm for twenty years, working every bit of it, ploughing it, harrowing it, weeding it carefully and then sells it, the purchaser is bound to reap good crops for some years to come; but if now the owner does not work the farm properly, the crops will fall off. Hon. gentlemen talk incessantly about the Country's prosperity and a buoyant revenue; why not show alongside the increase in the expenditure? I will say openly that expenses cannot but increase with a minister in the cabinet like Robert Rogers who wherever he has been has squandered the public money. As one instance, look at the public works undertaken in the county of Laprai-rie, which had to be rebuilt three or four times. Were they intended to benefit the people? No, but to get votes. It is useless for hon. members to attempt to inspire faith
in the present Government; our farmers are fully alive to what is going on here at Ottawa.
Now, in what position do we stand today? Last year, I .predicted for this year a net indebtness of $850,000,000 and a gross indebtedness of $1,200,000,000. I fell short of the truth; the Minister of Finance puts the present figures at $900,000,000 and $1,365,000,000 respectively; and predicts for the end of the present fiscal year an increase in [DOT] each case to $1,300,000,000 and $1,700,000,000 to $1,800,000,000. Who dare talk of prosperity when the expenditure exceeds three or four times our revenue?
You, Mr. Speaker, represent as I do a farming constituency; could you convince a farmer of Chambly-Vercheres that a man is more prosperous when he borrows money than otherwise. Will you get a serious man to believe all the stuff that is meted out in newspapers such as " La Presse " and " La Patrio " of Montreal, papers paid by the Government to deceive the people? Do you think the electors are not better informed? At any rate those in my constituency know better and I take care that they be informed as to what is being done at Ottawa. With another year of war-I fear that unfortunately, it may last longer than we wish -what will our debt amount to? The people have a right to know the whole truth. I have no hesitation to state, knowing that I am stating to the House and to my electors what is true, that after the war the national debt will amount to not less than three billions of dollars. Are the munitions of war included in the figures given out by the Minister of Finance last week? Shall we not have to settle with the Imperial Government after the war? If I am rightly informed, there is an agreement whereby the Canadian Government will reimburse to the Imperial authorities for the upkeep of the Canadian soldiers an amount equivalent to six shillings per unit per day. In that case, how many millions shall we have to hand over to the Imperial Government after the war? To this expenditure, which will fill the people with dismay, add the cost bf expropriating the railways for, according to the report of the commissioners tabled a few days ago, they are mostly all bankrupt and sooner or later the Government will have to take them over. No small sum to add to our Budget. It were better for tin* Government to rent the roads at one dollar a year for a period of twenty years or more and put at the head a capable manager like Shaughnessy and run the roads at reasonable rates. Now, Mr. Speaker, I had a few more things to say that I expected would be of interest to my honourable friend from Chft-teauguay; as he is not in his seat, I shall cut my remarks short. A word about recruiting. I am quite aware that to-morrow the Ontario press, headed by the Orange Sentinel and the News, will publish that the member for Laprairie has made an attack against the Empire. I deny it. The member for Laprairie is just as devoted to the Empire as those who vilify and calumniate the member for Laprairie. For many months past we are told in the press that, recruiting is at a standstill throughout the country; that immense sums are spent for the sake of a few recruits enlisted here and there. A host of recruiting agents are employed. The same thing takes place in the province of Quebec; lieutenant-colonels, majors, captains and others that I forget, not (being versed in military matters, are

mating vain efforts. On this point, I have a final suggestion to make to the Government: If you wish to have a battalion to go to the front under Lieutenant-Colonel Blondin, it is all ready. Just gather together the (recruiting agents,, (for whom there is no further utility -and as an appreciation of their work s-end them overseas. There is Mr. Blondin'-s opportunity to satisfy his desire of going to battle.
I wish to express my thanks to the House for their kind attention, especially at such a late hour of the night.
